solution.misconception: Using 2^(n²) for every property. Each constraint removes free pairs and shrinks the exponent.
solution.faster: Count the free pairs first: irreflexive relations on n elements number 2^(n²−n).
solution.takeaway: Compute the exponent as the number of pairs still free, not the size of A × A.

questions.question: How many relations on a set with four elements are both reflexive and antisymmetric?

solution.concept: Reflexivity fixes the diagonal pairs; antisymmetry constrains each unordered off-diagonal pair to at most one direction.
steps: Reflexivity forces all 4 diagonal pairs to be present — 1 way.
The 12 off-diagonal pairs fall into 6 unordered pairs {a, b}.
For each unordered pair, antisymmetry permits exactly three states: neither directed pair, only (a,b), or only (b,a).
Total 3⁶ = 729.
why_wrong: (A) 2⁶ = 64 is the reflexive-and-symmetric count, where each unordered pair is both-or-neither.
(B) 6³ = 216 uses 3 choices but only 3 unordered pairs.
(D) 2¹² = 4096 counts all reflexive relations, ignoring antisymmetry.
solution.misconception: Giving each unordered pair two choices. Antisymmetry leaves three, because either direction may be present or neither.
solution.faster: Reflexive and antisymmetric on n elements number 3^(n(n−1)/2).
solution.takeaway: Reflexive fixes n pairs; antisymmetric contributes 3 options per unordered off-diagonal pair.

questions.question: How many partial orders are there on a set with three elements?

solution.concept: A partial order is a reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive relation; on three labelled elements it is best counted by the shape of its Hasse diagram.
steps: Antichain (no comparabilities): 1 order.
Exactly one comparable pair: choose the two elements and the direction, 3 · 2 = 6.
A chain of three: 3! = 6 linear orders.
A V shape: one minimal element below two incomparable elements — choose the minimum, 3 orders.
A Λ shape: one maximal element above two incomparable elements — choose the maximum, 3 orders.
Total 1 + 6 + 6 + 3 + 3 = 19.
why_wrong: (A) 12 counts only the chains and the V/Λ shapes.
(C) 27 is the number of reflexive and antisymmetric relations, which ignores transitivity.
(D) 33 double-counts the shapes that are also chains.
solution.misconception: Counting reflexive antisymmetric relations and assuming transitivity is automatic. It is not: {(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,2),(2,3)} is reflexive and antisymmetric but not transitive.
solution.faster: Classify by Hasse-diagram shape — antichain, one edge, chain, V, Λ — and multiply by the number of ways to place each shape.
solution.takeaway: Counting posets means counting Hasse-diagram shapes, not pair selections.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about counting relations on a set A with |A| = n are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Every relation on A is a subset of A × A, and every subset of A × A is a relation on A.
The number of symmetric relations on A is 2^(n(n+1)/2).
The number of antisymmetric relations on A is 2^(n(n−1)/2).
A reflexive relation on A contains exactly n² − n ordered pairs.

solution.concept: Relations on A correspond exactly to subsets of A × A, so counting relations means counting free choices over the pairs of A × A.
steps: (A) is the definition; the correspondence is a bijection. TRUE.
(B) A symmetric relation is free on the n diagonal pairs and on the n(n−1)/2 unordered off-diagonal pairs, so 2^(n + n(n−1)/2) = 2^(n(n+1)/2). TRUE.
(C) fails: antisymmetry allows three states per unordered off-diagonal pair, giving 2ⁿ · 3^(n(n−1)/2).
(D) fails: reflexivity forces at least the n diagonal pairs and says nothing about the off-diagonal ones, so any number from n up to n² is possible.
why_wrong: (C) swaps the symmetric and antisymmetric formulas. Symmetric uses 2 choices per pair, antisymmetric uses 3.
(D) confuses a lower bound with an exact count.
solution.misconception: Assuming symmetric and antisymmetric relations are counted by the same expression. The antisymmetric count carries an extra factor 2ⁿ.
solution.faster: Symmetric → 2 choices per unordered pair; antisymmetric → 3 choices per unordered pair.
solution.takeaway: Symmetric relations: 2^(n(n+1)/2). Antisymmetric relations: 2ⁿ · 3^(n(n−1)/2).

questions.question: Let R = {(1,2), (2,3), (3,1)} on A = {1, 2, 3}. Which of the following equals R ∘ R?

solution.concept: R ∘ R advances every walk by one step: (x,z) lies in R ∘ R exactly when a path of length two runs from x to z.
steps: (1,2) then (2,3) gives (1,3).
(2,3) then (3,1) gives (2,1).
(3,1) then (1,2) gives (3,2).
why_wrong: (B) is R itself. Having (1,2) in the composition would need a y with (1,y) ∈ R and (y,2) ∈ R, and no such y exists.
(C) is the diagonal, which appears only in R³.
(D) ignores the three two-step walks.
solution.misconception: Assuming %s whenever %s is a cycle. Composition shifts the cycle by one step instead of returning it.
solution.faster: For a single directed cycle of length 3, R² is the same cycle rotated and R³ is the diagonal.
solution.takeaway: Here R³ = I_A, so the transitive closure is R ∪ R² ∪ R³ = A × A.

questions.question: Let f : ℤ → ℤ be defined by f(x) = 2x. Which one of the following describes f correctly?
options: f is injective but not surjective.
f is surjective but not injective.
f is neither injective nor surjective.

solution.concept: Injectivity asks whether two different inputs can share an output; surjectivity asks whether every element of the codomain is hit at all. On infinite domains the two are independent.
steps: Suppose f(a) = f(b), i.e. 2a = 2b. Dividing by 2 gives a = b, so f is injective.
Now take the codomain element 3. If 2x = 3 then x = 3/2, which is not an integer, so 3 has no preimage in ℤ.
More generally only even integers are values of f, so the image is 2ℤ ⊊ ℤ.
Hence f is injective and not surjective.
why_wrong: (A) fails: odd integers such as 3 are never attained, so f is not onto.
(C) fails: doubling is one-to-one, so it is not "onto but not one-to-one".
(D) fails: injectivity is already proved in step 1.
solution.misconception: Students transfer the finite-set rule "injective ⇔ surjective" to ℤ. That equivalence needs the domain and codomain to be finite of equal size; on infinite sets x ↦ 2x is injective but leaves half the codomain untouched.
solution.faster: Check surjectivity first with a single odd target such as 3. One missing preimage settles the question, and injectivity of a linear map is immediate from the slope.
solution.takeaway: On infinite sets, injective does not imply surjective: the classic witness is f(x) = 2x on ℤ.

questions.question: Let ℤ⁺ = {1, 2, 3, …}. Which one of the following functions f : ℤ⁺ → ℤ⁺ is surjective (onto)?

solution.concept: A function into ℤ⁺ is surjective when every positive integer occurs as a value. For a candidate, the quickest test is to try to hit a small target such as 1.
steps: (A) n + 1 ≥ 2 for every n ≥ 1, so 1 is never attained. Not surjective.
(B) 2n is even, so 1 (and every odd number) is missed. Not surjective.
(C) ⌈n/2⌉ takes the values 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, … for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, …. Every k ∈ ℤ⁺ is attained, for instance at n = 2k − 1. Surjective.
(D) n² attains only perfect squares, so 2 is missed. Not surjective.
why_wrong: (A) and (B) are strictly increasing with image bounded below by 2 and by the even numbers respectively.
(D) misses every non-square.
solution.misconception: Assuming a "spreading out" function such as 2n covers everything because it grows. Growth is irrelevant to surjectivity; what matters is which values are hit.
solution.faster: For each option, ask "can it produce 1?" Only (C) can.
solution.takeaway: ⌈n/2⌉ is the standard example of a surjective non-injective map on ℤ⁺.

questions.question: Let A and B be finite sets with |A| = |B| = n ≥ 1, and let f : A → B. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: If f is injective, then f is bijective.
If f is surjective, then f is bijective.
Every function f : A → B is bijective.
If f is bijective, then f has an inverse function f⁻¹ : B → A.

solution.concept: For a function between finite sets of equal size, injective, surjective and bijective are the same condition. That is the pigeonhole principle in disguise.
steps: If f is injective, its n inputs give n distinct outputs inside an n-element codomain, so every element of B is used: f is also surjective, hence bijective. (A) is TRUE.
If f is surjective, all n elements of B are hit; n hits from n inputs with no repeats is impossible unless each output is hit exactly once. So f is injective, hence bijective. (B) is TRUE.
(C) is FALSE: with A = B = {1, 2}, the constant map f ≡ 1 is a function but not bijective.
A bijection has an inverse: f⁻¹(y) is the unique x with f(x) = y. (D) is TRUE.
why_wrong: (C) is the trap: existence of a function is not existence of a bijection. Most maps between equal finite sets are not bijections.
solution.misconception: Reading "injective implies bijective" as a universal law. It holds only because |A| = |B| is finite; drop either hypothesis and it fails.
solution.faster: Memorise the finite equal-cardinality triangle: injective ⇔ surjective ⇔ bijective. Then (A) and (B) are immediate and (C) is obviously too strong.
solution.takeaway: On finite sets of equal size, one-to-one and onto are the same test; on infinite sets they are not.

questions.question: Let f : ℝ → ℝ be defined by f(x) = x / (x² + 1). Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: f is injective but not surjective.
f is surjective but not injective.
f is neither injective nor surjective.

solution.concept: Injectivity is destroyed by a single collision f(a) = f(b) with a ≠ b. Surjectivity onto ℝ is destroyed by showing the range is bounded.
steps: Collision: f(2) = 2/5 and f(1/2) = (1/2)/(5/4) = 2/5. Since 2 ≠ 1/2, f is not injective.
In general f(x) = f(1/x) for x ≠ 0, so every value away from 0 is taken at least twice.
Range: by AM–GM, x² + 1 ≥ 2|x|, so |f(x)| ≤ 1/2, with equality at x = ±1.
Values such as 1 lie outside [−1/2, 1/2], so f is not surjective onto ℝ.
Therefore f is neither injective nor surjective.
why_wrong: (A) fails because of the collision f(2) = f(1/2).
(B) fails because the range is confined to [−1/2, 1/2].
(D) fails on both counts.
solution.misconception: Testing injectivity only with integers, or assuming a bounded, symmetric-looking curve must still be one-to-one. The symmetry f(x) = f(1/x) is exactly what breaks injectivity.
solution.faster: Boundedness settles surjectivity in one line. For injectivity, look for symmetry: any f with f(x) = f(1/x) or f(x) = f(−x) is immediately non-injective.
solution.takeaway: A function can fail injectivity (symmetry) and surjectivity (bounded range) at the same time; check each property separately.

questions.question:
Let f : ℝ → ℝ be defined by f(x) = x² − 4x + 7. How many real numbers x satisfy f(x) = 3?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Solving f(x) = c is solving a quadratic; the number of solutions is the number of distinct real roots, which the discriminant decides.
steps: Set x² − 4x + 7 = 3.
Rearrange: x² − 4x + 4 = 0.
Factor: (x − 2)² = 0, so x = 2 is a double root.
The discriminant is 16 − 16 = 0, confirming exactly one distinct real solution.
solution.misconception: Counting the double root twice and answering 2. "How many real numbers x" asks for distinct solutions, so a repeated root counts once.
solution.faster: Complete the square first: f(x) = (x−2)² + 3. Then f(x) = 3 ⇔ (x−2)² = 0, giving the answer at a glance and also showing the minimum value is 3.
solution.takeaway: Vertex form (x − h)² + k tells you both the range and how many preimages a value has: below k none, at k exactly one, above k two.

questions.question: Let f, g : ℝ → ℝ with f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = x². Then (f ∘ g)(x) equals

solution.concept: (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)): the right-hand function acts first, and its output becomes the input of the left-hand function.
steps: (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)) = f(x²).
Substitute x² into f(u) = 2u + 3: f(x²) = 2x² + 3.
why_wrong: (A) is (g ∘ f)(x) = (2x + 3)², the composition in the other order.
(C) and (D) square the wrong coefficient or add the wrong term; neither follows from substituting x² into 2u + 3.
solution.misconception: Applying f first. Composition is read right to left: in f ∘ g, g goes first.
solution.faster: Write the outer function with a blank: 2( ) + 3, then drop g(x) into the blank.
solution.takeaway: f ∘ g ≠ g ∘ f in general; here the two orders give 2x² + 3 and 4x² + 12x + 9.

questions.question: Let f : A → B and g : B → C. Suppose g ∘ f : A → C is injective. Which one of the following must be TRUE?

solution.concept: Injectivity of a composite forces injectivity of the first map applied, but says nothing about the second.
steps: Suppose f(a₁) = f(a₂). Applying g gives g(f(a₁)) = g(f(a₂)), i.e. (g∘f)(a₁) = (g∘f)(a₂).
Injectivity of g ∘ f then gives a₁ = a₂. Hence f is injective. (A) holds.
Counterexample for g: A = {1}, B = {p, q}, C = {r}, f(1) = p, g(p) = g(q) = r. Then g ∘ f is injective but g is not, so (B) fails.
Surjectivity is untouched: with A = B = C = {1} and identity maps everything is injective and surjective; with B = {p, q} above, f is not surjective, so (C) fails.
why_wrong: (B) fails by the two-element counterexample above: g may collapse elements of B that f never reaches.
(C) and (D) are about surjectivity, which composition does not force from injectivity.
solution.misconception: Concluding that g is injective because g ∘ f is. g only has to be injective on the image of f, not on all of B.
solution.faster: Remember the two legal deductions: g∘f injective ⇒ f injective, and g∘f surjective ⇒ g surjective. The other two implications are false.
solution.takeaway: Injectivity propagates backwards through a composite (to the first map); surjectivity propagates forwards (to the second).

questions.question: Let f : A → B and g : B → C. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: If f and g are both injective, then g ∘ f is injective.
If f and g are both surjective, then g ∘ f is surjective.
If g ∘ f is surjective, then g is surjective.
If g ∘ f is injective, then g is injective.

solution.concept: Composition preserves both injectivity and surjectivity when both factors have the property, and the composite can also pass a property back to one factor.
steps: (A) If (g∘f)(a₁) = (g∘f)(a₂), injectivity of g gives f(a₁) = f(a₂) and injectivity of f gives a₁ = a₂. TRUE.
(B) Take any c ∈ C. Surjectivity of g gives b ∈ B with g(b) = c; surjectivity of f gives a ∈ A with f(a) = b. Then (g∘f)(a) = c. TRUE.
(C) The image of g ∘ f is g(f(A)) ⊆ g(B). If g(f(A)) = C then certainly g(B) = C. TRUE.
(D) FALSE: take A = {1}, B = {p, q}, C = {r}, f(1) = p, g(p) = g(q) = r. Then g∘f is injective but g is not.
why_wrong: (D) reverses the correct direction: injectivity of the composite passes back to the first factor f, not to g.
solution.misconception: Assuming every property is inherited in both directions. Composition preserves injective/injective and surjective/surjective forwards, but passes a property back to only one factor.
solution.faster: Picture the arrows: A → B → C. Anything that must "not collide" is inherited by the map leaving A; anything that must "cover" is inherited by the map entering C.
solution.takeaway: g∘f injective ⇒ f injective; g∘f surjective ⇒ g surjective; both properties are preserved by composing two maps that have them.

questions.question: Let f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = x² be functions on ℝ, and put h = g ∘ f, k = f ∘ g. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: The equation h(x) = k(x) holds for exactly one real x.
Both h and k are injective.
k ∘ h = h ∘ k as functions.

solution.concept: Two composites of the same pair of functions generally differ; comparing them means writing both in closed form and solving, and remembering that x² is not injective.
steps: h(x) = g(f(x)) = (x + 1)² and k(x) = f(g(x)) = x² + 1. They are different functions, so (A) is false.
h(x) = k(x) ⇔ x² + 2x + 1 = x² + 1 ⇔ 2x = 0 ⇔ x = 0. Exactly one solution, so (B) is true.
k(1) = k(−1) = 2, so k is not injective and (C) is false.
k(h(x)) = ((x+1)²)² + 1 = (x+1)⁴ + 1 while h(k(x)) = (x² + 1 + 1)² = (x² + 2)². At x = 0 these are 2 and 4, so (D) is false.
solution.final: Option (B) — exactly one real solution, x = 0.
why_wrong: (A) fails since h(1) = 4 but k(1) = 2.
(C) fails because squaring destroys injectivity.
(D) fails at x = 0, where the two iterates differ.
solution.misconception: Assuming g ∘ f = f ∘ g for "simple" functions, or that composing twice is automatically commutative. Composition is associative but almost never commutative.
solution.faster: Compare at a single convenient point first: h(0) = 1, k(0) = 1 (so 0 is a candidate root); h(1) = 4, k(1) = 2 (so they are different). Then solve the difference, which is linear here.
solution.takeaway: g∘f and f∘g can agree at isolated points without being equal functions; expanding both sides usually leaves a linear equation.

questions.question:
Let f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = 3x + 1 be bijections on ℝ. Find the value of (f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹)(16).
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: To evaluate f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹, apply the right-hand inverse first: undo g, then undo f. Equivalently use (g ∘ f)⁻¹ = f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹.
steps: Inverses: f⁻¹(y) = (y − 1)/2 and g⁻¹(y) = (y − 1)/3.
Apply g⁻¹ first: g⁻¹(16) = (16 − 1)/3 = 5.
Then apply f⁻¹: f⁻¹(5) = (5 − 1)/2 = 2.
Check with the other route: (g ∘ f)(x) = 3(2x + 1) + 1 = 6x + 4, and 6x + 4 = 16 gives x = 2. Both routes agree.
solution.misconception: Applying f⁻¹ first, which computes (g⁻¹ ∘ f⁻¹)(16) = g⁻¹(7.5) = 13/6 — a different number. In f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹ the function written on the right acts first, exactly as in ordinary composition.
solution.faster: Solve (g ∘ f)(x) = 16 directly: 6x + 4 = 16 gives x = 2 in one line.
solution.takeaway: (g ∘ f)⁻¹ = f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹: inverting a composite reverses the order, and the order matters.

questions.question: Let |A| = 4 and |B| = 3. How many functions f : A → B are there?

solution.concept: A function A → B is an independent choice of one codomain element for each domain element, so the count is |B|^|A|.
steps: Each of the 4 elements of A may map to any of the 3 elements of B.
The choices are independent, so multiply: 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 3⁴ = 81.
why_wrong: (A) 12 is |A| · |B|, which counts pairs, not functions.
(B) 24 counts the injective functions only.
(D) 64 is 4³, the count with the sizes swapped.
solution.misconception: Swapping the exponent: the domain size is the exponent, the codomain size is the base.
solution.faster: Say it out loud: "for each of the 4 inputs, 3 choices" → 3⁴.
solution.takeaway: Number of functions A → B is |B|^|A|.

questions.question: Let |A| = 4 and |B| = 5. How many injective functions f : A → B are there?

solution.concept: An injective function picks distinct images for the domain elements in turn, so the count is a falling factorial |B|(|B|−1)…(|B|−|A|+1).
steps: The first element of A has 5 possible images.
The second must avoid that one: 4 choices. The third: 3 choices. The fourth: 2 choices.
Multiply: 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 = 120.
why_wrong: (A) 20 is 5 × 4, the count if |A| were 2.
(C) 625 is 5⁴, the count of all functions, which includes the non-injective ones.
(D) 24 is 4!, the count of bijections when |A| = |B| = 4.
solution.misconception: Using |B|^|A| and forgetting the distinctness constraint, or using P(5,5) instead of P(5,4).
solution.takeaway: Injective functions A → B: P(|B|, |A|), and 0 when |A| > |B|.

questions.question: Let |A| = 3 and |B| = 4. Which of the following counts are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: There are 64 functions f : A → B.
There are 24 injective functions f : A → B.
There are 0 surjective functions f : A → B.
There are 24 bijections f : A → B.

solution.concept: Counts follow the size comparison: all functions |B|^|A|, injective P(|B|,|A|), surjective 0 whenever |A| < |B|, bijections 0 whenever |A| ≠ |B|.
steps: All functions: 4³ = 64. (A) TRUE.
Injective: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24. (B) TRUE.
Surjective: 3 inputs can hit at most 3 of the 4 codomain elements, so none. (C) TRUE.
Bijections require equal sizes; 3 ≠ 4, so there are 0, not 24. (D) FALSE.
why_wrong: (D) is the trap: 24 is the number of injections, and every injection here is far from a bijection because two codomain elements are left unused.
solution.misconception: Equating "injective count" with "bijection count". They coincide only when the two sets have equal size.
solution.faster: First compare sizes. Smaller domain → no surjection; unequal sizes → no bijection. That eliminates (C) and (D) instantly, leaving two arithmetic checks.
solution.takeaway: With |A| < |B|: |B|^|A| functions, P(|B|,|A|) injections, no surjections, no bijections.

questions.question: Let |A| = 5 and |B| = 3. How many surjective functions f : A → B are there?

solution.concept: Count onto maps by inclusion–exclusion over the codomain elements that are missed: Σ (−1)^k C(n,k) (n−k)^m for m inputs and n targets.
steps: Total functions: 3⁵ = 243.
Subtract those missing at least one target. Missing a fixed target leaves 2⁵ = 32 functions, and there are C(3,1) = 3 choices of the missed target: 3 × 32 = 96.
Add back the double subtractions. Missing two fixed targets leaves 1⁵ = 1 function, with C(3,2) = 3 such pairs: 3.
Nothing misses all three targets. So the count is 243 − 96 + 3 = 150.
why_wrong: (A) 90 is 3! · S(5,3) = 6 · 15 — that counts onto maps up to relabelling of the codomain, then multiplies, but S(5,3) = 25, not 15, so 90 is the wrong product.
(B) 125 is 5³, the count with the sizes swapped.
(D) 243 is 3⁵, all functions, including the 93 that miss something.
solution.misconception: Using S(m,n) alone. The Stirling number counts partitions of the domain, so the number of onto maps is n! · S(m,n) = 6 × 25 = 150; forgetting the n! factor (or using a wrong Stirling value) is the usual error.
solution.faster: S(5,3) = 25 from the Stirling triangle, then 3! × 25 = 150. Cross-check with inclusion–exclusion as above.
solution.takeaway: Surjections from an m-set onto an n-set: n! S(m,n), equivalently Σ(−1)^k C(n,k)(n−k)^m.

questions.question:
How many bijections are there from a set with 6 elements onto itself?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: A bijection from a finite set onto itself is a permutation of its elements, so the count is n!.
steps: Choose the image of element 1: 6 ways.
Choose the image of element 2 from what is left: 5 ways, and so on down to 1 way for the last element.
Multiply: 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 720.
solution.misconception: Counting 6⁶ (all functions) or 2⁶. A bijection must use each element exactly once, which is a permutation, not an arbitrary assignment.
solution.faster: 6! = 720; memorise factorials up to 10! = 3628800.
solution.takeaway: Bijections of an n-set to itself = n!; between two different n-sets also n!.

questions.question: What is the minimum number of people in a room that guarantees at least three of them were born in the same month?

solution.concept: To force k + 1 objects into one of m boxes, you need km + 1 objects: with only km you could place exactly k in every box.
steps: Here m = 12 months and we want k + 1 = 3, so k = 2.
The bound is 2 × 12 + 1 = 25.
Sharpness: 24 people can be spread with exactly 2 per month, so 24 is not enough. With 25 people some month receives at least ⌈25/12⌉ = 3.
why_wrong: (A) 13 forces only two in a month: ⌈13/12⌉ = 2.
(B) 24 is the largest number that avoids three in a month, so it does not guarantee it.
(D) 27 works but is not the minimum.
solution.misconception: Answering 24 because "2 per month is 24". That is exactly the configuration to be avoided; the guarantee needs one more.
solution.faster: ⌈N/12⌉ ≥ 3 ⇔ N > 24 ⇔ N ≥ 25.
solution.takeaway: Guaranteeing k+1 in some box of m boxes needs km + 1 objects — never km.

questions.question: Let f be a function from a set with 10 elements into a set with 9 elements. Which one of the following must be TRUE?
options: Some element of the codomain is the image of at least two domain elements.
Exactly one codomain element is the image of exactly two domain elements.

solution.concept: Pigeonhole: 10 objects in 9 boxes force some box to hold at least two. It says nothing about which box, or about how the rest are distributed.
steps: The 10 domain elements are assigned to 9 codomain elements.
If every codomain element were the image of at most one element, the image would contain 10 distinct values inside a 9-element set — impossible.
So some codomain element is hit at least twice. (B) holds.
Nothing forces surjectivity: the map could send all 10 elements to one value and leave 8 values unused. So (C) fails, and (A) fails too.
Nothing forces the excess to be exactly 2: f could send 3 elements to one value. So (D) fails.
solution.final: Option (B) — some codomain element is hit at least twice.
why_wrong: (A) is impossible here: injectivity needs at least 10 codomain elements.
(C) fails for the constant function, which is a perfectly legal map.
(D) is too specific: a 3-to-1 collision is equally allowed.
solution.misconception: Strengthening the conclusion from "at least two" to "exactly two". The pigeonhole principle gives an inequality, not a distribution.
solution.faster: Compare sizes: 10 > 9, so no injection; that kills (A) and, with a one-line constant-function counterexample, kills (C) and (D).
solution.takeaway: Pigeonhole conclusions are "at least", never "exactly"; and no injection exists as soon as the domain is larger than the codomain.

questions.question: Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: In any group of 13 people, at least two share a birth month.
In any group of 25 people, at least three share a birth month.
In any group of 24 people, at least three share a birth month.
If 11 numbers are chosen from {1, 2, …, 20}, two of them are consecutive.

solution.concept: Each claim is a pigeonhole count: identify the objects, the boxes, and how many objects force a given occupancy.
steps: (A) 13 people, 12 months: ⌈13/12⌉ = 2, so some month holds at least two. TRUE.
(B) 25 people: ⌈25/12⌉ = 3. TRUE.
(C) 24 people can occupy the 12 months exactly two at a time, so three is not forced. FALSE.
(D) Split {1, …, 20} into the 10 pairs {1,2}, {3,4}, …, {19,20}. Choosing 11 numbers means two come from the same pair, and those two are consecutive. TRUE.
why_wrong: (C) is the boundary case: 24 = 2 × 12 is achievable with two per month, so it guarantees nothing beyond two.
solution.misconception: Treating 24 as "close enough" to force three, and forgetting to build the boxes in (D). For (D) the boxes are the consecutive pairs, not the numbers themselves.
solution.faster: For each claim, compute ⌈N/m⌉ and compare with the claimed occupancy; for (D), partition the range into the relevant pairs.
solution.takeaway: Pigeonhole questions are decided by the right choice of boxes: months, pairs, residues, or subsquares.

questions.question: Given any 5 integers, which one of the following is guaranteed?
options: Some three of them have a sum divisible by 3.
Some two of them have a sum divisible by 3.
Some four of them have a sum divisible by 3.
Their total sum is divisible by 3.

solution.concept: Work modulo 3. Only the residues matter, and there are just three of them, so a short case analysis on how the five residues are distributed settles everything.
steps: Reduce the five integers modulo 3, giving five residues in {0, 1, 2}.
Case 1: some residue class contains at least three of them. Three integers with the same residue r sum to 3r ≡ 0 (mod 3). Done.
Case 2: no class has three. With five residues over three classes, the counts must be (2, 2, 1) in some order.
Then one element has each residue 0, 1, 2, and 0 + 1 + 2 = 3 ≡ 0 (mod 3). Done.
So a suitable triple always exists, and (A) is guaranteed.
solution.final: Option (A) — some three have a sum divisible by 3.
why_wrong: (B) fails: take all five equal to 1; every pair sums to 2, which is not divisible by 3.
(C) fails for the same five 1s: four of them sum to 4.
(D) fails for the same five 1s: the total is 5.
solution.misconception: Stopping after Case 1. The interesting case is the "balanced" distribution (2, 2, 1), where no class is large but one element of each residue still gives a multiple of 3.
solution.faster: Check the two shapes of a 5-element multiset of residues: a class of size ≥ 3, or the balanced (2,2,1) split. Both give a zero-sum triple, so the claim is immediate.
solution.takeaway: Any 5 integers contain three whose sum is a multiple of 3; the extremal configuration is all five congruent, which already satisfies the claim.

questions.question:
What is the smallest number n such that among any n integers there are always two whose difference is divisible by 9?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: "Difference divisible by 9" means the two integers are congruent modulo 9, so the boxes are the 9 residue classes and the objects are the chosen integers.
steps: Two integers differ by a multiple of 9 exactly when they share a residue modulo 9. There are 9 residues, i.e. 9 boxes.
With 9 integers we can pick one from each class, e.g. 0, 1, …, 8, and no two share a residue. So n = 9 is not enough.
With 10 integers, two must fall in the same class, and their difference is divisible by 9.
Hence the smallest such n is 10.
solution.misconception: Answering 9 because there are 9 residue classes. Nine objects can occupy nine boxes one each; the guarantee needs one more object than there are boxes.
solution.faster: The answer is always (number of boxes) + 1: here 9 + 1 = 10.
solution.takeaway: For "two congruent modulo m" the threshold is m + 1; the extremal example is one representative per residue class.

questions.question: For a real number x, the value of ⌈x⌉ − ⌊x⌋ is
options: 0 when x is an integer, and 1 otherwise
0 when x is an integer, and −1 otherwise

solution.concept: ⌊x⌋ is the largest integer not exceeding x; ⌈x⌉ is the smallest integer not less than x. Their difference measures the fractional part.
steps: If x ∈ ℤ, then ⌊x⌋ = ⌈x⌉ = x, so the difference is 0.
If x ∉ ℤ, write x = k + f with k ∈ ℤ and 0 < f < 1. Then ⌊x⌋ = k and ⌈x⌉ = k + 1.
So the difference is 1 exactly for non-integers.
Check: x = 2.3 gives 3 − 2 = 1; x = −2.3 gives −2 − (−3) = 1; x = 5 gives 0.
why_wrong: (A) and (C) each fail for one of the two cases: (A) at x = 2.3, (C) at x = 5.
(D) never occurs: ⌈x⌉ ≥ ⌊x⌋ always, so the difference is never negative.
solution.misconception: Handling negative numbers wrongly. For x = −2.3, ⌊x⌋ = −3 and ⌈x⌉ = −2; the difference is still 1, not −1.
solution.faster: The difference is the indicator of "x is not an integer" — worth memorising, together with ⌊x⌋ + ⌈−x⌉ = 0.
solution.takeaway: ⌈x⌉ − ⌊x⌋ ∈ {0, 1}, equal to 0 exactly on the integers.

questions.question: How many integers from 1 to 1000 (both inclusive) are divisible by neither 3 nor 5?

solution.concept: Counting "neither" is inclusion–exclusion on the complement: subtract the multiples of 3 and of 5, then add back the multiples of 15 that were removed twice.
steps: Multiples of 3 up to 1000: ⌊1000/3⌋ = 333.
Multiples of 5: ⌊1000/5⌋ = 200.
Multiples of 15 (counted in both lists): ⌊1000/15⌋ = 66.
Divisible by 3 or 5: 333 + 200 − 66 = 467.
Neither: 1000 − 467 = 533.
why_wrong: (A) 466 forgets to add back the 66 multiples of 15.
(C) 534 is off by one, the usual fencepost slip.
(D) 600 is 1000 minus the 400 multiples of 5 and 3 counted separately without the overlap correction.
solution.misconception: Subtracting 333 and 200 and stopping: the 66 multiples of 15 get removed twice, so the total of "divisible by 3 or 5" is overstated and the "neither" count is understated by 66.
solution.faster: 1000 − 333 − 200 + 66 = 533; note the alternating signs and use floor division only.
solution.takeaway: For "neither a nor b" up to N: N − ⌊N/a⌋ − ⌊N/b⌋ + ⌊N/lcm(a,b)⌋.

questions.question: Which of the following identities hold for ALL real numbers x and y? (Select all that apply.)

solution.concept: Negation swaps floor and ceiling; floors add sub-additively, never super-additively.
steps: (A) True: reflecting about 0 turns the greatest integer below x into the least integer above −x. Test x = 2.3: ⌊−2.3⌋ = −3 = −⌈2.3⌉.
(B) True: the same reflection the other way. Test x = 2.3: ⌈−2.3⌉ = −2 = −⌊2.3⌋.
(C) False: at x = 0.4, ⌊0.9⌋ = 0 but ⌈0.4⌉ = 1.
(D) True: ⌊x⌋ ≤ x and ⌊y⌋ ≤ y, so ⌊x⌋ + ⌊y⌋ ≤ x + y; the left side is an integer, hence it is at most ⌊x + y⌋.
why_wrong: (C) is a near-identity that fails for fractional parts below ½; it holds only when {x} ≥ ½.
solution.misconception: Believing ⌊x + y⌋ = ⌊x⌋ + ⌊y⌋. It can differ by 1 (take x = y = 0.6) but the left side is never smaller.
solution.faster: Test each identity at a fractional value such as x = 0.4 and at a negative value: most false identities die at once.
solution.takeaway: ⌊−x⌋ = −⌈x⌉, ⌈−x⌉ = −⌊x⌋, and ⌊x⌋ + ⌊y⌋ ≤ ⌊x + y⌋ ≤ ⌊x⌋ + ⌊y⌋ + 1.

questions.question: Let f(0) = 1 and f(n) = f(⌊n/2⌋) + 1 for every integer n ≥ 1. Then f(1000) equals

solution.concept: Unrolling a recurrence that halves its argument counts how many halvings are needed to reach 0, i.e. the number of bits of n plus one.
steps: f(125) = f(62) + 1, f(62) = f(31) + 1, f(31) = f(15) + 1, f(15) = f(7) + 1, f(7) = f(3) + 1, f(3) = f(1) + 1, f(1) = f(0) + 1 = 2.
Closed form: f(n) = ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 2 for n ≥ 1. Here ⌊log₂ 1000⌋ = 9 since 2⁹ = 512 ≤ 1000 < 1024 = 2¹⁰, so f(1000) = 11.
why_wrong: (A) 10 forgets the base case f(0) = 1 and counts only the halvings.
(C) 12 and (D) 13 over-count by one or two, typically by rounding log₂ 1000 ≈ 9.97 up and then adding the base twice.
solution.misconception: Using log₂1000 ≈ 9.97 → 10 and then answering 10. The recurrence counts halvings with floor division, and the base case contributes the extra 1.
solution.faster: Count the bits: 1000 = 1111101000₂ has 10 bits, so the number of halvings to reach 0 is 10 and f = 10 + 1 = 11.
solution.takeaway: For f(n) = f(⌊n/2⌋) + c, f(n) = c⌊log₂ n⌋ + f(0) + c on n ≥ 1.

questions.question:
A sequence is defined by T(1) = 1 and T(n) = T(⌊n/2⌋) + n for n ≥ 2. Find T(8).
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Unroll the recurrence from the top down, replacing each argument by its floor half until the base case is reached, then add the contributions on the way back up.
steps: T(8) = T(4) + 8.
T(4) = T(2) + 4.
T(2) = T(1) + 2 = 1 + 2 = 3.
So T(4) = 3 + 4 = 7 and T(8) = 7 + 8 = 15.
Check with the sum form: T(8) = 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15, since the arguments along the chain are the powers of two down to the base case.
solution.misconception: Adding the halved values (4 + 2 + 1) instead of the original arguments, which gives 8 rather than 15; in this recurrence the added term is n, the current argument.
solution.faster: For n = 2^k the chain is 2^k, 2^{k−1}, …, 1, so T(2^k) = 2^{k+1} − 1. With k = 3: T(8) = 16 − 1 = 15.
solution.takeaway: Unroll small recurrences explicitly; for power-of-two arguments the answer is a geometric sum n + n/2 + n/4 + … + 1 = 2n − 1.

questions.sub: Images and preimages of a shift on the naturals
questions.question: Let ℕ = {0, 1, 2, …} and let f : ℕ → ℕ be defined by f(n) = n + 5. Which one of the following describes f correctly?
options: f is injective but not surjective.
f is surjective but not injective.
f is neither injective nor surjective.

solution.concept: A shift of the natural numbers is one-to-one, but the first few codomain values are simply never produced. Injectivity and surjectivity are separate tests and a shift passes only the first.
steps: If f(a) = f(b) then a + 5 = b + 5, so a = b: f is injective.
The image is {5, 6, 7, …}: the values 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 are never attained.
So f is not surjective, and it is injective but not surjective.
solution.misconception: Students see a bijection of ℤ (namely n ↦ n + 5) and assume the same map is a bijection of ℕ. Shifting destroys surjectivity because ℕ has a first element and nothing maps onto the bottom five values.
solution.takeaway: On ℕ a shift is injective but never onto; only on ℤ does it become a bijection.

questions.sub: Surjectivity versus injectivity of a cubic
questions.question: Let f : ℝ → ℝ be defined by f(x) = x³ − x. Which one of the following describes f correctly?
options: f is injective but not surjective.
f is surjective but not injective.
f is neither injective nor surjective.

solution.concept: An odd-degree polynomial has full range ℝ (surjective), but it is injective only if it is monotone. A cubic with two turning points folds back on itself and therefore repeats values.
steps: f(0) = 0 and f(1) = 0, so two different inputs share an output: f is not injective.
f′(x) = 3x² − 1, which vanishes at x = ±1/√3; these are the two turning points.
As x → +∞, f(x) → +∞ and as x → −∞, f(x) → −∞; being continuous, f takes every real value, so it is surjective.
Hence f is surjective but not injective.
solution.misconception: Assuming an odd-degree polynomial is automatically a bijection. Odd degree guarantees surjectivity only; injectivity needs monotonicity, which x³ − x lacks.
solution.takeaway: Odd degree ⇒ onto. Monotone ⇒ one-to-one. x³ − x is the standard example of onto-but-not-one-to-one.

questions.question: Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: f : ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = x³ is bijective.
f : ℤ → ℤ, f(n) = n² is injective.
f : ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = eˣ is injective.
f : ℝ → [0, ∞), f(x) = x² is surjective.

solution.concept: Each option tests one side of the injective/surjective split on a specific codomain. Changing the codomain changes surjectivity; changing the domain changes injectivity.
steps: (A) x³ is strictly increasing on ℝ, so it is injective; it is continuous with limits ±∞, so its range is ℝ and it is surjective. TRUE.
(B) f(1) = f(−1) = 1, so two inputs share an output. FALSE.
(C) eˣ is strictly increasing, hence injective. (It is not surjective onto ℝ, but the option claims only injectivity.) TRUE.
(D) For every y ≥ 0, f(√y) = y, so the codomain [0, ∞) is fully covered. TRUE.
solution.misconception: Rejecting (C) because eˣ misses the negative numbers. Surjectivity is not being claimed there — and rejecting (D) because x² is not injective on ℝ. Each option names one property only.
solution.takeaway: Surjectivity is a property of the map together with its codomain; the same formula can be onto one codomain and not another.

questions.sub: Strict monotonicity from a non-negative derivative
questions.question: Let f : ℝ → ℝ be defined by f(x) = x + sin x. Which one of the following describes f correctly?
options: f is injective but not surjective.
f is surjective but not injective.
f is neither injective nor surjective.

solution.concept: A differentiable function is strictly increasing when its derivative is non-negative and vanishes only at isolated points. A strictly increasing continuous function with infinite limits at both ends is a bijection of ℝ.
steps: f′(x) = 1 + cos x ≥ 0 for all x, and f′(x) = 0 only at x = (2k+1)π, a discrete set with no interval in between.
So f is strictly increasing: x₁ < x₂ implies f(x₁) < f(x₂). Hence f is injective.
As x → +∞, x + sin x ≥ x − 1 → +∞; as x → −∞, x + sin x ≤ x + 1 → −∞.
f is continuous, so by the intermediate value theorem it takes every real value: f is surjective.
Injective and surjective, therefore bijective.
solution.misconception: Because sin x oscillates, students expect f to oscillate too and to be non-injective. The linear term dominates: the derivative 1 + cos x never becomes negative, so the function never turns around.
solution.takeaway: x + sin x is the standard example of a strictly increasing function whose derivative is not always positive — monotone does not require f′ > 0 everywhere.

questions.sub: Counting bijections among a family of test functions
questions.question: How many of the following six functions f : ℝ → ℝ are bijections?f₁(x) = 2x + 1, f₂(x) = x², f₃(x) = x³, f₄(x) = |x|, f₅(x) = eˣ, f₆(x) = x³ − x(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: A bijection of ℝ onto ℝ must be both one-to-one and onto. Even-degree powers and absolute values fold the line; the exponential escapes the negative range; a cubic with turning points folds locally.
steps: f₁(x) = 2x + 1: linear with non-zero slope, range ℝ. Bijection. (1)
f₂(x) = x²: f(1) = f(−1) = 1, so not injective; range [0, ∞), so not surjective either. Not a bijection.
f₃(x) = x³: strictly increasing, range ℝ. Bijection. (2)
f₄(x) = |x|: f(1) = f(−1) = 1, not injective; range [0, ∞), not surjective. No.
f₅(x) = eˣ: injective, but the range is (0, ∞), so −1 is never attained. Not onto.
f₆(x) = x³ − x: f(0) = f(1) = 0, so not injective (it is onto). No.
Total: f₁ and f₃ only, so the answer is 2.
solution.misconception: Counting eˣ as a bijection because it has an inverse function ln x. The inverse exists on (0, ∞) only — eˣ : ℝ → ℝ is injective but not onto, so it is not a bijection of ℝ.
solution.takeaway: Of the six classic test functions, only 2x + 1 and x³ are bijections of ℝ onto ℝ.

questions.sub: Evaluating a composite at a point
questions.question: Let f(x) = x + 2 and g(x) = 3x be functions on ℝ. Then (g ∘ f)(x) equals

solution.concept: Composition applies the right-hand function first: (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)). Substitute f(x) into g, not the other way round.
steps: Compute f first: f(x) = x + 2.
Feed that value into g: g(x + 2) = 3(x + 2).
Expand: 3x + 6.
solution.misconception: Reading (g ∘ f)(x) left to right as g then f. The composition symbol is applied right to left: the function nearest the argument runs first.
solution.takeaway: (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)): inner function first. (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)) = 3x + 2 is a different function.

questions.sub: Inverse pairs on a restricted domain
questions.question: Let f(x) = x² and g(x) = √x both be defined on [0, ∞) with codomain [0, ∞). Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: f and g are inverse functions of each other on [0, ∞).
There is some x ≥ 0 with (f ∘ g)(x) ≠ (g ∘ f)(x).

solution.concept: Two functions are inverses when both compositions are the identity on the relevant domains. Restricting x² to [0, ∞) is exactly what makes √x a genuine inverse.
steps: (f ∘ g)(x) = (√x)² = x for every x ≥ 0, since √x ≥ 0.
(g ∘ f)(x) = √(x²) = |x| = x for every x ≥ 0.
Both compositions are the identity on [0, ∞), so f and g are mutually inverse there.
solution.final: Option (B) — they are inverses of each other on [0, ∞).
solution.misconception: Quoting √(x²) = |x| and concluding the two compositions differ. That identity is about all real x; on the restricted domain [0, ∞) we have |x| = x, so the compositions coincide.
solution.takeaway: x² on [0, ∞) and √x on [0, ∞) are true inverses; x² on ℝ is not injective and has no inverse.

questions.sub: Associativity, commutativity and inverse of a composite
questions.question: Which of the following statements about composition and inverses are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Composition is associative: (f ∘ g) ∘ h = f ∘ (g ∘ h) whenever all the compositions are defined.
f ∘ g = g ∘ f whenever both compositions are defined.
If f : A → B is a bijection, then f ∘ f⁻¹ is the identity on B.
If f and g are bijections, then (f ∘ g)⁻¹ = g⁻¹ ∘ f⁻¹.

solution.concept: Composition behaves like multiplication of functions: associative, generally not commutative, and the inverse of a product reverses the order.
steps: (A) Both sides send x to f(g(h(x))). TRUE.
(B) Take f(x) = x + 1, g(x) = x². Then (f∘g)(1) = 2 while (g∘f)(1) = 4. FALSE.
(C) (f ∘ f⁻¹)(y) = f(f⁻¹(y)) = y for every y ∈ B. TRUE.
(D) (f ∘ g)(g⁻¹ ∘ f⁻¹) = f ∘ (g ∘ g⁻¹) ∘ f⁻¹ = f ∘ f⁻¹ = identity, and similarly on the other side. TRUE.
solution.misconception: Assuming that because matrix multiplication is associative and non-commutative in the same way, function composition behaves identically in every respect — in particular, that the inverse of f ∘ g is f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹. The order must reverse.
solution.takeaway: Composition: associative, not commutative, and (f ∘ g)⁻¹ = g⁻¹ ∘ f⁻¹ with the order reversed.

questions.sub: One-sided identity versus a genuine inverse pair
questions.question: Let f : ℤ → ℤ be f(x) = 2x and g : ℤ → ℤ be g(x) = ⌊x/2⌋. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: f and g are inverse bijections of each other.
g ∘ f is the identity on ℤ, but f ∘ g is not; and f is not surjective.
Both g ∘ f and f ∘ g are the identity on ℤ.

solution.concept: One composition being the identity forces only one of the two functions to be injective and the other surjective. Two functions are mutual inverses only when both compositions are the identity.
steps: (g ∘ f)(x) = ⌊2x/2⌋ = ⌊x⌋ = x for every integer x. So g ∘ f is the identity on ℤ.
(f ∘ g)(x) = 2⌊x/2⌋, which equals x when x is even and x − 1 when x is odd. So f ∘ g is not the identity.
Indeed f ∘ g is not injective: (f ∘ g)(0) = 0 and (f ∘ g)(1) = 0.
f(x) = 2x has image 2ℤ, so odd integers are never attained: f is not surjective.
Hence (B) holds; (A) and (C) fail because the second composition is not the identity.
solution.misconception: Concluding from g ∘ f = id that f and g are inverses. A one-sided identity gives f injective and g surjective only — here f misses the odd integers and g identifies 2k with 2k + 1, so neither is a bijection.
solution.takeaway: g ∘ f = id ⇏ f and g are inverse bijections. It gives only f injective and g surjective; the other composition must be checked separately.

questions.sub: Inverting a composite of linear maps
questions.question: Let f(x) = 2x − 1 and g(x) = x + 3 be bijections on ℝ. Find (g ∘ f)⁻¹(8).(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Two routes give the same answer: invert the composite directly, or use (g ∘ f)⁻¹ = f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹ and work backwards through g then f.
steps: First find the composite: (g ∘ f)(x) = g(2x − 1) = (2x − 1) + 3 = 2x + 2.
Solve 2x + 2 = 8, giving 2x = 6 and x = 3.
Check by the inverse-order route: g⁻¹(y) = y − 3 gives g⁻¹(8) = 5; f⁻¹(y) = (y + 1)/2 gives f⁻¹(5) = 3. Both agree.
solution.misconception: Evaluating g⁻¹ first and then f⁻¹ the wrong way round, i.e. computing f⁻¹(g⁻¹(8)) with f⁻¹ applied first. The composite (g ∘ f)⁻¹ is f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹, so g⁻¹ acts first.
solution.takeaway: (g ∘ f)⁻¹ = f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹; for linear functions the direct route through the composite is usually quicker.

questions.sub: Counting all functions between finite sets
questions.question: Let |A| = 3 and |B| = 5. How many functions f : A → B are there?

solution.concept: A function makes an independent choice of image for each of the |A| domain elements, with |B| options each time. The count is |B|^|A|, not |A|·|B|.
steps: Each of the 3 elements of A independently picks one of the 5 elements of B.
By the product rule the number of functions is 5 × 5 × 5 = 5³.
solution.misconception: Confusing |B|^|A| with |A|^|B|. The exponent is the size of the domain, because each domain element makes a choice.
solution.takeaway: Functions A → B: |B|^|A|. Functions B → A: |A|^|B|. Here 5³ = 125, not 3⁵ = 243.

questions.sub: Injections when the domain is larger than the codomain
questions.question: Let |A| = 5 and |B| = 3. How many injective functions f : A → B are there?

solution.concept: An injection needs at least as many codomain points as domain points. When |A| > |B| the pigeonhole principle makes an injection impossible, so the count is 0.
steps: An injective f would send 5 distinct domain elements to 5 distinct codomain elements.
But B has only 3 elements, so 5 distinct images cannot fit.
By the pigeonhole principle no injective map exists; the count is 0.
solution.misconception: Mechanically applying P(|B|, |A|) and getting a negative or nonsensical product. The formula P(n, r) is defined only for r ≤ n; here r = 5 > n = 3, so the honest answer is 0.
solution.takeaway: Injections A → B: P(|B|, |A|) when |A| ≤ |B|, and 0 otherwise. Size comparison comes before any formula.

questions.sub: Comparing function, injection, surjection and bijection counts
questions.question: Let |A| = 2 and |B| = 4. Which of the following counts are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: There are 16 functions f : A → B.
There are 12 injective functions f : A → B.
There are 0 surjective functions f : A → B.
There are 12 bijections f : A → B.

solution.concept: The four counts follow from the size comparison: |B|^|A| functions, P(|B|, |A|) injections, and no surjection or bijection when |A| < |B|.
steps: Functions: 4² = 16. (A) TRUE.
Injections: P(4, 2) = 4 × 3 = 12. (B) TRUE.
Surjections: two inputs can hit at most two codomain elements, so with |B| = 4 at least two elements are missed. Count 0. (C) TRUE.
Bijections require |A| = |B|; here 2 ≠ 4, so the count is 0, not 12. (D) FALSE.
solution.misconception: Reading 'injective' and 'bijective' as interchangeable on unequal sets. With |A| < |B| an injection exists but can never be onto, so no bijection exists.
solution.takeaway: Unequal finite sizes: injections may exist, surjections and bijections cannot (in the direction A → B with |A| < |B|).

questions.question: Let |A| = 6 and |B| = 3. How many surjective functions f : A → B are there?

solution.concept: Count the complement with inclusion–exclusion: subtract the maps that miss at least one codomain element, add back the double-counted ones. The answer is Σ(−1)ᵏ C(n,k)(n−k)^m for m = |A|, n = |B|.
steps: Total functions: 3⁶ = 729.
Maps missing a fixed element of B: 2⁶ = 64 each, and there are C(3,1) = 3 of them: subtract 3 × 64 = 192.
Maps missing two fixed elements (i.e. constant maps): 1⁶ = 1 each, C(3,2) = 3 of them: add back 3.
Surjective count = 729 − 192 + 3 = 540.
solution.misconception: Computing 3! · S(6,3) correctly as 540 but stopping at 3⁶ − 3·2⁶ = 537 and forgetting the +3 correction. Inclusion–exclusion must alternate signs all the way down.
solution.takeaway: Onto functions from an m-set to an n-set: n! S(m,n) = Σ(−1)ᵏ C(n,k)(n−k)^m. Here 540.

questions.sub: Counting non-bijections on a finite set
questions.question: How many functions f : {1, 2, 3, 4} → {1, 2, 3, 4} are NOT bijections?(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Count all functions on a 4-element set and subtract the bijections. A function from a finite set to itself is a bijection exactly when it is a permutation.
steps: Total functions: 4⁴ = 256.
Bijections on 4 elements: 4! = 24.
Non-bijections: 256 − 24 = 232.
solution.misconception: Answering 256 − 4 = 252, subtracting the number of elements instead of the number of permutations. There are 24 bijections, not 4.
solution.takeaway: On a finite set, 'bijection' = 'permutation'. Non-bijections = nⁿ − n!.

questions.question: What is the minimum number of students needed to guarantee that at least two of them were born on the same day of the week?

solution.concept: With m boxes, m + 1 objects force a collision. The days of the week are the 7 boxes.
steps: Treat the 7 weekdays as boxes and the students as objects.
With 7 students it is possible for each to fall in a different box — no guarantee.
With 8 students, 8 > 7 forces two into the same box by the pigeonhole principle.
solution.misconception: Answering 7 by analogy with '7 days'. The guarantee needs one more object than there are boxes, so the threshold is 7 + 1 = 8.
solution.takeaway: For 'at least two in the same category' with m categories the threshold is m + 1, never m.

questions.sub: Worst-case argument for a matching pair
questions.question: A drawer holds 10 red, 10 blue and 10 green socks. Drawing in the dark, what is the smallest number of socks that guarantees a matching pair (two of the same colour)?

solution.concept: The worst case before a collision is one sock of every colour. One more sock than there are colours forces a repeat.
steps: There are 3 colours, so 3 boxes.
Worst case: draw one red, one blue and one green — 3 socks, still no pair.
The 4th sock must repeat one of the three colours, giving a matching pair.
solution.misconception: Using the 10 socks per colour as the box count. The boxes here are colours (3), not socks. Separately, guaranteeing a specific colour does need 21.
solution.takeaway: 'Some pair' uses colours as boxes (4 socks); 'a pair of a named colour' uses all the other socks as the worst case (21).

questions.question: Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Among any 5 integers, two leave the same remainder on division by 4.
Among any 6 integers, two differ by a multiple of 5.
Among any 4 integers, two differ by a multiple of 4.
Among any 13 integers, two leave the same remainder on division by 12.

solution.concept: Two integers differ by a multiple of k exactly when they share a remainder mod k. So the question is always: how many objects can share k boxes before a collision is forced?
steps: (A) 5 objects, 4 residues: 5 > 4, so a collision is forced. TRUE.
(B) 6 objects, 5 residues mod 5: 6 > 5, forced. TRUE.
(C) 4 objects, 4 residues mod 4: the integers 0, 1, 2, 3 occupy all four residues with no repeat. FALSE.
(D) 13 objects, 12 residues: 13 > 12, forced. TRUE.
solution.misconception: Assuming any k integers must collide mod k. The threshold is k + 1; with exactly k integers a clean one-per-class arrangement always exists.
solution.takeaway: k + 1 integers force two with the same residue mod k; k integers need not.

questions.sub: Generalised pigeonhole bound on a grid colouring
questions.question: Each cell of a 10 × 10 grid is coloured with one of 4 colours. Which one of the following must be TRUE?
options: Some colour is used on at least 25 cells.
Some colour is used on at least 26 cells.
Every colour is used on exactly 25 cells.
No colour is used on more than 30 cells.

solution.concept: With 100 objects in 4 boxes, the average is 25, so the largest box has at least ⌈100/4⌉ = 25. The bound is tight: a perfectly even split attains it, so no larger universal guarantee is possible.
steps: There are 100 cells and 4 colours: 100 objects, 4 boxes.
If every colour were used on at most 24 cells, the total would be at most 4 × 24 = 96 < 100, a contradiction.
So some colour covers at least 25 cells. (A) is TRUE.
Colour the grid in four 5 × 5 blocks of 25 cells each: no colour then reaches 26, so (B) is not guaranteed.
An uneven split such as 40, 20, 20, 20 refutes (C), and a monochromatic grid refutes (D).
solution.misconception: Upgrading 'at least 25' to 'at least 26'. The generalised pigeonhole principle gives ⌈N/k⌉ = ⌈100/4⌉ = 25 exactly, and 25 is attained, so any larger claim is false.
solution.takeaway: Generalised pigeonhole: some box holds at least ⌈N/k⌉ objects. When N is a multiple of k, that bound is the best possible.

questions.sub: Largest guaranteed group size from a ceiling
questions.question: In a class of 40 students, what is the largest k such that some birth month is guaranteed to contain at least k of them?(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: The generalised pigeonhole principle guarantees a box with at least ⌈N/m⌉ objects, and that bound is the largest guaranteed value.
steps: So some month holds at least 4 students — the guarantee cannot fail.
It is tight: 40 = 12 × 3 + 4, so 4 months can hold 4 students and the remaining 8 months 3 each, with no month reaching 5.
solution.misconception: Rounding down to 3 with ⌊40/12⌋. The pigeonhole principle rounds up: if every month held at most 3, only 36 students could be placed.
solution.takeaway: Largest guaranteed group size = ⌈N/m⌉, and it is attained, so no larger value can be promised.

questions.sub: Floor and ceiling on a negative argument
questions.question: For the real number x = −3.4, the value of ⌊x⌋ + ⌈x⌉ is

solution.concept: For negative arguments the floor rounds down (more negative) and the ceiling rounds up (towards zero). They are not symmetric about zero.
steps: ⌊−3.4⌋ is the greatest integer ≤ −3.4, namely −4.
⌈−3.4⌉ is the least integer ≥ −3.4, namely −3.
solution.misconception: Truncating towards zero, i.e. reading ⌊−3.4⌋ as −3. Floor always moves left on the number line, so a negative non-integer floors to the next more negative integer.
solution.takeaway: On negatives, floor goes away from zero and ceiling goes towards zero; only ⌊x⌋ ≤ x ≤ ⌈x⌉ is safe to rely on.

questions.sub: Block of integers attaining a given floor value
questions.question: How many integers n with 1 ≤ n ≤ 100 satisfy ⌊n/3⌋ = 12?

solution.concept: ⌊n/3⌋ = k exactly when k ≤ n/3 < k + 1, i.e. 3k ≤ n ≤ 3k + 2. Each value of k is attained by exactly 3 consecutive integers.
steps: The integers are 36, 37, 38.
All three lie in 1 ≤ n ≤ 100, so the count is 3.
solution.misconception: Reading ⌊n/3⌋ = 12 as n = 36 only. A floor value is attained on a whole block of three integers, and the right endpoint is excluded.
solution.takeaway: ⌊n/d⌋ = k ⟺ kd ≤ n ≤ kd + d − 1: exactly d consecutive integers.

questions.sub: Inequalities and sub-additivity for floor and ceiling
questions.question: Which of the following hold for ALL real numbers x and y? (Select all that apply.)

solution.concept: Floor and ceiling bracket the argument: ⌊x⌋ ≤ x ≤ ⌈x⌉. Ceiling is superadditive and floor is subadditive; the floor identity fails whenever the fractional parts sum to 1 or more.
steps: (A) ⌈x⌉ is by definition an integer ≥ x. TRUE.
(B) ⌊x⌋ is by definition an integer ≤ x. TRUE.
(D) ⌈x⌉ ≥ x and ⌈y⌉ ≥ y, so ⌈x⌉ + ⌈y⌉ ≥ x + y. The left side is an integer, hence it is at least ⌈x + y⌉. TRUE.
solution.misconception: Assuming floor distributes over addition. The correct one-way inequalities are ⌊x⌋ + ⌊y⌋ ≤ ⌊x + y⌋ and ⌈x⌉ + ⌈y⌉ ≥ ⌈x + y⌉; equality is not general.
solution.takeaway: Floor is subadditive, ceiling is superadditive, and both bracket their argument. Distributive laws for + fail.

questions.question: Let T(1) = 1 and T(n) = 2T(⌊n/2⌋) + n for n ≥ 2. Then T(8) equals

solution.concept: Unroll a halving recurrence on a power of two: the argument halves each level, so only about log₂ n levels exist and the terms form a geometric series.
steps: Cross-check with the closed form T(n) = n log₂ n + n for powers of two: 8 × 3 + 8 = 32, agreeing with the unrolling.
solution.misconception: Plugging into the Master Theorem and reporting Θ(n log n) as though it were the value at n = 8. The asymptotic form hides constants; a numerical question needs the recurrence unrolled.
solution.takeaway: For power-of-two arguments, unroll level by level. T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n with T(1) = 1 gives the exact value n log₂ n + n, so T(8) = 24 + 8 = 32.

questions.sub: Counting integers in a floor-of-square-root block
questions.question: How many integers n with 1 ≤ n ≤ 200 satisfy ⌊√n⌋ = 11?(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: ⌊√n⌋ = k exactly when k² ≤ n < (k + 1)², so the value k is attained on a block of 2k + 1 consecutive integers.
steps: That is 121 ≤ n ≤ 143.
The count is 143 − 121 + 1 = 23.
All of these lie inside 1 ≤ n ≤ 200, so nothing is excluded.
solution.misconception: Computing 144 − 121 = 23 and then doubting it, or writing 22 by forgetting the inclusive left endpoint. The block is 121 … 143, which is 23 integers.
solution.takeaway: ⌊√n⌋ = k is attained on exactly 2k + 1 integers, from k² to (k+1)² − 1.

questions.subject: discrete-mathematics
questions.question: For every integer n ≥ 1, the sum ∑_{i=1}^{n} i·2ⁱ is given by which one of the following closed forms?
questions.question_html: For every integer n ≥ 1, the sum ∑_{i=1}^{n} i·2ⁱ is given by which one of the following closed forms?
options_html: (n − 1)2ⁿ⁺¹ + 2
(n + 1)2ⁿ⁺¹ − 2
n·2ⁿ⁺¹ − 2ⁿ
(n − 1)2ⁿ + 2

solution.concept: A sum of the form ∑ i·2ⁱ is proved by ordinary induction: assume the closed form for n = k, then add the single new term (k+1)2^{k+1} and simplify back into the same shape with k replaced by k+1. The first term gives the base case.
steps: Base case n = 1: the sum is 1·2 = 2. Option (A) gives (0)·4 + 2 = 2, option (B) gives 2·4 − 2 = 6, option (C) gives 1·4 − 2 = 2, option (D) gives 0 + 2 = 2. So (B) is already out, and three options survive n = 1.
Second value n = 2: the sum is 2 + 8 = 10. (A) gives (1)·8 + 2 = 10; (C) gives 2·8 − 4 = 12; (D) gives 1·4 + 2 = 6. Only (A) survives.

Inductive step (confirmation): assume ∑_{i=1}^{k} i·2ⁱ = (k−1)2^{k+1} + 2. Then ∑_{i=1}^{k+1} = (k−1)2^{k+1} + 2 + (k+1)2^{k+1} = 2k·2^{k+1} + 2 = k·2^{k+2} + 2, which is the same formula with k replaced by k+1.
why_wrong: (B) gives 6 at n = 1, not 2.
(C) agrees at n = 1 but gives 12 at n = 2, not 10.
(D) agrees at n = 1 but gives 6 at n = 2, not 10.
solution.misconception: Checking only n = 1 accepts three of the four options, because several formulas agree on the first value. Two test values (or a genuine induction step) are needed; this is exactly why a base case alone never proves a closed form.
solution.faster: Compute the sum at n = 1 and n = 2 — the pair (2, 10) — and eliminate. Only (A) matches both.
solution.takeaway: For a claimed closed form, evaluate at two small values first and only then write the induction step.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A sum of the form ∑ i·2ⁱ is proved by ordinary induction: assume the closed form for n = k, then add the single new term (k+1)2^{k+1} and simplify back into the same shape with k replaced by k+1. The first term gives the base case.

Step by step.

  1. Base case n = 1: the sum is 1·2 = 2. Option (A) gives (0)·4 + 2 = 2, option (B) gives 2·4 − 2 = 6, option (C) gives 1·4 − 2 = 2, option (D) gives 0 + 2 = 2. So (B) is already out, and three options survive n = 1.
  2. Second value n = 2: the sum is 2 + 8 = 10. (A) gives (1)·8 + 2 = 10; (C) gives 2·8 − 4 = 12; (D) gives 1·4 + 2 = 6. Only (A) survives.
  3. Inductive step (confirmation): assume ∑_{i=1}^{k} i·2ⁱ = (k−1)2^{k+1} + 2. Then ∑_{i=1}^{k+1} = (k−1)2^{k+1} + 2 + (k+1)2^{k+1} = 2k·2^{k+1} + 2 = k·2^{k+2} + 2, which is the same formula with k replaced by k+1.

Answer: Option (A) — (n − 1)2ⁿ⁺¹ + 2.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) gives 6 at n = 1, not 2.
  • (C) agrees at n = 1 but gives 12 at n = 2, not 10.
  • (D) agrees at n = 1 but gives 6 at n = 2, not 10.

Common misconception. Checking only n = 1 accepts three of the four options, because several formulas agree on the first value. Two test values (or a genuine induction step) are needed; this is exactly why a base case alone never proves a closed form.

Faster method. Compute the sum at n = 1 and n = 2 — the pair (2, 10) — and eliminate. Only (A) matches both.

Takeaway. For a claimed closed form, evaluate at two small values first and only then write the induction step.

questions.subject: discrete-mathematics
questions.question: For each integer n ≥ 1 let P(n) be the statement 2ⁿ > n². A student takes n = 1 as the only base case and claims that P(k) ⇒ P(k+1) holds for every k ≥ 1. The smallest value of k for which that implication is false is
questions.question_html: For each integer n ≥ 1 let P(n) be the statement 2ⁿ > n². A student takes n = 1 as the only base case and claims that P(k) ⇒ P(k+1) holds for every k ≥ 1. The smallest value of k for which that implication is false is

solution.concept: An induction step is an implication P(k) ⇒ P(k+1) that must be true for every k in the range. It can fail either because P(k+1) is false while P(k) is true — that is a failure of the step itself, and no amount of base-case work can repair it.
steps: P(1): 2¹ = 2 > 1 = 1², so P(1) is true.
P(2): 2² = 4 > 4 = 2² is false. Therefore P(1) ⇒ P(2) is a true antecedent with a false consequent, so the implication fails at k = 1.
P(3): 8 > 9 is also false, so the step fails at k = 2 as well; the first failure is nevertheless at k = 1.
The claim itself is false for n = 2 and n = 3 and true for n = 1 and for all n ≥ 5, so this statement cannot be proved by induction starting at n = 1 at all.
why_wrong: (B) k = 2 is a second failure, not the smallest one.
(C) and (D): at k = 3 and k = 4 the implication is true (P(3) is false, which makes the implication vacuously true, and P(4) ⇒ P(5) is 16 > 16 false ⇒ 32 > 25 true, again vacuously true).
solution.misconception: Students check the step at a large k, where it works, and conclude the proof is fine. The step must be checked for every k in the range, including the smallest one — and when the step fails, changing the base case cannot help.
solution.faster: Evaluate P(1) and P(2). The very first implication is already false, so the answer is k = 1.
solution.takeaway: The base case and the step are separate obligations: here the base case holds and the step fails immediately.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An induction step is an implication P(k) ⇒ P(k+1) that must be true for every k in the range. It can fail either because P(k+1) is false while P(k) is true — that is a failure of the step itself, and no amount of base-case work can repair it.

Step by step.

  1. P(1): 2¹ = 2 > 1 = 1², so P(1) is true.
  2. P(2): 2² = 4 > 4 = 2² is false. Therefore P(1) ⇒ P(2) is a true antecedent with a false consequent, so the implication fails at k = 1.
  3. P(3): 8 > 9 is also false, so the step fails at k = 2 as well; the first failure is nevertheless at k = 1.
  4. The claim itself is false for n = 2 and n = 3 and true for n = 1 and for all n ≥ 5, so this statement cannot be proved by induction starting at n = 1 at all.

Answer: Option (A) — k = 1.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) k = 2 is a second failure, not the smallest one.
  • (C) and (D): at k = 3 and k = 4 the implication is true (P(3) is false, which makes the implication vacuously true, and P(4) ⇒ P(5) is 16 > 16 false ⇒ 32 > 25 true, again vacuously true).

Common misconception. Students check the step at a large k, where it works, and conclude the proof is fine. The step must be checked for every k in the range, including the smallest one — and when the step fails, changing the base case cannot help.

Faster method. Evaluate P(1) and P(2). The very first implication is already false, so the answer is k = 1.

Takeaway. The base case and the step are separate obligations: here the base case holds and the step fails immediately.

questions.subject: discrete-mathematics
questions.question:
Using the identity ∑_{i=1}^{n} i³ = (n(n+1)/2)², the value of ∑_{i=1}^{10} i³ is ______.
(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
Using the identity ∑_{i=1}^{n} i³ = (n(n+1)/2)², the value of ∑_{i=1}^{10} i³ is ______.
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: The identity is the induction-friendly form of the sum of cubes: the closed form is the square of the sum of the first n integers. Once the closed form is known, the numeric answer is one substitution.
steps: Sum of the first 10 integers: 1 + 2 + … + 10 = 10·11/2 = 55.
Square it: 55² = 3025.
solution.misconception: Forgetting the division by 2 and computing 110² = 12100, or squaring only the last term. The base of the square is the whole sum n(n+1)/2.
solution.faster: 55² = 3025 — the whole question is one arithmetic step once the identity is recognised.
solution.takeaway: ∑ i³ = (∑ i)²; the closed form is a square, so the answer is a perfect square.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The identity is the induction-friendly form of the sum of cubes: the closed form is the square of the sum of the first n integers. Once the closed form is known, the numeric answer is one substitution.

Step by step.

  1. Sum of the first 10 integers: 1 + 2 + … + 10 = 10·11/2 = 55.
  2. Square it: 55² = 3025.
  3. Cross-check with the cube values: 1 + 8 + 27 + 64 + 125 + 216 + 343 + 512 + 729 + 1000 = 3025.

Answer: 3025.

Common misconception. Forgetting the division by 2 and computing 110² = 12100, or squaring only the last term. The base of the square is the whole sum n(n+1)/2.

Faster method. 55² = 3025 — the whole question is one arithmetic step once the identity is recognised.

Takeaway. ∑ i³ = (∑ i)²; the closed form is a square, so the answer is a perfect square.

questions.subject: discrete-mathematics
questions.question: Which one of the following statements about strong (complete) induction and ordinary (weak) induction on ℕ is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following statements about strong (complete) induction and ordinary (weak) induction on ℕ is TRUE?
options: Strong induction can prove statements that ordinary induction cannot, because it assumes more.
Every statement provable by strong induction is also provable by ordinary induction.
A strong-induction proof needs no base case, because the hypothesis already covers the earlier values.
A strong-induction proof must verify at least two base cases before the step can be applied.
options_html: Strong induction can prove statements that ordinary induction cannot, because it assumes more.
Every statement provable by strong induction is also provable by ordinary induction.
A strong-induction proof needs no base case, because the hypothesis already covers the earlier values.
A strong-induction proof must verify at least two base cases before the step can be applied.

solution.concept: Strong induction assumes P(0), P(1), …, P(k) and concludes P(k+1); ordinary induction assumes only P(k). The two principles prove exactly the same set of statements, because ordinary induction applied to the auxiliary claim Q(n) = “P(j) holds for all j ≤ n” reproduces the strong step.
steps: Assume every statement provable by strong induction is provable by weak induction is what has to be shown. Let P be provable by strong induction. Define Q(n) as “P(0) ∧ P(1) ∧ … ∧ P(n)”.
The strong step gives P(0) ∧ … ∧ P(k) ⇒ P(k+1), which is exactly Q(k) ⇒ Q(k+1). The base case P(0) gives Q(0).
Ordinary induction on Q therefore gives Q(n) for all n, hence P(n) for all n. So strong induction adds no theorems.
The converse is immediate: a weak step is a special case of the strong step.

options: In a strong-induction proof, replacing the hypothesis “P(j) holds for every j ≤ k” by “P(k) holds” may leave the proof invalid.

questions.question: A statement P(n) is to be proved for every integer n ≥ 0, and the inductive step derives P(n+1) from P(n) and P(n−1) together. The minimum number of base cases the proof must verify is
questions.question_html: A statement P(n) is to be proved for every integer n ≥ 0, and the inductive step derives P(n+1) from P(n) and P(n−1) together. The minimum number of base cases the proof must verify is

solution.concept: A step that reaches back r values cannot prove the first r values, so r base cases are needed. Here the step at n = k needs P(k) and P(k−1), which exist only from k = 1 onwards.
steps: Apply the step at n = 0: it would need P(0) and P(−1). P(−1) is outside the range, so the step cannot run at n = 0.
Apply the step at n = 1: it needs P(1) and P(0). Both must already be known.
Therefore P(0) and P(1) must be verified directly — two base cases. From n = 2 onwards the step runs.
One base case would leave P(1) unproved, so the chain would break at the very first link; three is more than the minimum.
solution.misconception: Assuming one base case always suffices. The count is dictated by the step: a step that uses r earlier values needs r base cases, and with fewer the induction never starts.
solution.faster: Look at the smallest n at which the step can fire (here n = 1) and count the earlier values it needs (P(0), P(1)): that count is the number of base cases.
solution.takeaway: Number of base cases = how far back the inductive step reaches.

questions.question: For every integer n ≥ 1, the sum ∑_{k=1}^{n} k·k! equals
questions.question_html: For every integer n ≥ 1, the sum ∑_{k=1}^{n} k·k! equals
options_html: (n + 1)! − 1
(n + 1)! + 1
(n + 1)! − n
n!(n + 1)/2

solution.concept: The sum telescopes once each term is rewritten: k·k! = (k+1)! − k!, because (k+1)! = (k+1)·k! = k·k! + k!. Telescoping sums are the reason factorials and powers appear in induction questions.
steps: Rewrite the general term: k·k! = (k+1)! − k!.
Sum both sides from k = 1 to n: every intermediate factorial cancels, leaving (n+1)! − 1! = (n+1)! − 1.
Check small values: n = 1 gives 1 = 2! − 1 = 1; n = 2 gives 1 + 4 = 5 = 3! − 1 = 5; n = 3 gives 5 + 18 = 23 = 4! − 1 = 23.
Inductive step as an alternative: if the sum to k is (k+1)! − 1, adding (k+1)(k+1)! gives (k+2)(k+1)! − 1 = (k+2)! − 1.
why_wrong: (B) is off by 2 at n = 1 (3 instead of 1).
(C) agrees at n = 1 by accident but gives 4 at n = 2 instead of 5.
(D) agrees at n = 1 (1) but gives 3 at n = 2 instead of 5; the growth is polynomial, not factorial.
solution.misconception: Missing the −1. The telescoping sum collapses to (n+1)! minus the very first factorial, 1! = 1; forgetting that leftover term is the standard slip.
solution.faster: Spot k·k! = (k+1)! − k!. The sum then telescopes to (n+1)! − 1 in one line, and no induction is needed.
solution.takeaway: When a factorial sum appears, try writing each term as a difference of consecutive factorials; the sum then collapses.

questions.question: Let S be the smallest set of integers such that 1 ∈ S and x ∈ S ⇒ 2x ∈ S. To prove by structural induction that every element of S is a power of 2, the inductive step must be
questions.question_html: Let S be the smallest set of integers such that 1 ∈ S and x ∈ S ⇒ 2x ∈ S. To prove by structural induction that every element of S is a power of 2, the inductive step must be
options: assume 2ᵏ ∈ S and prove 2ᵏ⁺¹ ∈ S.
assume x ∈ S and x = 2ᵏ for some k ≥ 0, and prove that 2x = 2ᵏ⁺¹ is a power of 2.

solution.concept: Structural induction follows the definition: one base case per starting element, and one step per rule — assume the property for the rule's input and prove it for the rule's output. Here the input is x ∈ S and the output is 2x.
steps: The definition has one starting point, 1 ∈ S, and one rule, x ∈ S ⇒ 2x ∈ S. So there are two obligations.

Step: let x ∈ S and suppose x = 2ᵏ. Then 2x = 2^{k+1}, a power of 2. This is exactly option (B) — the property is assumed for the rule's input and proved for its output.

solution.faster: Find the rules of the definition. Each rule contributes exactly one obligation: hypothesis on its inputs, conclusion on its output.
solution.takeaway: Structural induction mirrors the definition: base elements give base cases, rules give steps from inputs to output.

questions.question:
A full binary tree is one in which every internal node has exactly two children. A full binary tree has 20 internal nodes. The total number of nodes in the tree is ______.
(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
A full binary tree is one in which every internal node has exactly two children. A full binary tree has 20 internal nodes. The total number of nodes in the tree is ______.
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Structural induction on the definition of a full binary tree gives the leaf–internal relation L = I + 1, and hence a total of 2I + 1 nodes. The proof works because a full binary tree is either a single leaf or a root with two full binary subtrees.
steps: Base case: the single-node tree has I = 0 internal nodes and L = 1 leaf, so L = I + 1.
Step: a tree with root r and subtrees T₁, T₂ has I = I₁ + I₂ + 1 and L = L₁ + L₂. By hypothesis L₁ = I₁ + 1 and L₂ = I₂ + 1, so L = I₁ + I₂ + 2 = (I₁ + I₂ + 1) + 1 = I + 1.
Total nodes = I + L = I + (I + 1) = 2I + 1.
solution.misconception: Answering 40 by forgetting the +1 (2I instead of 2I + 1), or 39 by using L = I − 1. The relation is L = I + 1 — leaves outnumber internal nodes by exactly one.
solution.faster: Every full binary tree with 20 internal nodes has 21 leaves; 20 + 21 = 41.
solution.takeaway: In a full binary tree, nodes = 2I + 1, leaves = I + 1, and both follow from one structural-induction step.

  4. With I = 20: total = 2(20) + 1 = 41.

questions.question: Let S be the smallest set of strings over {a, b} such that ε ∈ S and, for every w ∈ S, both awb and bwa belong to S. Which of the following statements are TRUE?
questions.question_html: Let S be the smallest set of strings over {a, b} such that ε ∈ S and, for every w ∈ S, both awb and bwa belong to S. Which of the following statements are TRUE?
options: Every w ∈ S contains the same number of a's and b's.
Every w ∈ S has even length.
options_html: Every w ∈ S contains the same number of a's and b's.
abba ∈ S.
Every w ∈ S has even length.
S is closed under concatenation.

solution.concept: Each rule of the definition wraps a string with one a and one b, so the two counts rise together — that is the structural-induction invariant. But an invariant is only a necessary condition; deciding membership needs the exact characterisation of S.
steps: (A) Base: ε has 0 a's and 0 b's. Step: awb adds one a and one b to w; bwa does the same. So #a(w) = #b(w) is preserved — true.
(C) Base: |ε| = 0, even. Step: |awb| = |w| + 2, so parity is preserved — true.

Exact description: a string of length 2m is in S exactly when its i-th symbol is the complement of its (2m+1−i)-th symbol (it equals the reverse of its own complement). Length 4 therefore gives exactly 0011-style patterns: aabb, abab, baba, bbaa.
(B) abba is not among them: reversing its complement gives baab ≠ abba. So abba ∉ S — false.
(D) ab ∈ S and ba ∈ S, but their concatenation abba ∉ S — false.
why_wrong: (B) fails: only four strings of length 4 lie in S — aabb, abab, baba, bbaa.
(D) fails: ab · ba = abba, which is not in S, so S is not closed under concatenation.
solution.misconception: Assuming the obvious invariant is also sufficient — here “equal numbers of a's and b's” is necessary but not sufficient, and abba is the witness. Structural induction proves invariants; it does not describe the set.
solution.faster: List S up to length 4 (ε, ab, ba, aabb, abab, baba, bbaa). Both true options and both counterexamples are then visible.
solution.takeaway: A property proved by structural induction is a necessary condition. Membership needs the exact characterisation, and the gap between them is a favourite exam trap.

questions.question:
Let S be the smallest set of positive integers such that 1 ∈ S and, for every x ∈ S, both 2x and 3x belong to S. How many elements of S are less than 20?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
Let S be the smallest set of positive integers such that 1 ∈ S and, for every x ∈ S, both 2x and 3x belong to S. How many elements of S are less than 20?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Structural induction gives the exact description of S: every element is reached from 1 by repeatedly multiplying by 2 or by 3, so S = {2^a·3^b : a, b ≥ 0}. Counting is then a small enumeration.
steps: Base: 1 = 2⁰·3⁰ ∈ S. Step: multiplying 2^a·3^b by 2 or by 3 gives 2^{a+1}·3^b or 2^a·3^{b+1}, again of the same form. So every element of S has that form.
Conversely every 2^a·3^b is generated by a multiplications by 2 and b by 3, so the description is exact.
Enumerate those below 20: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 16, 18.
The next candidates are 2·18 = 36, 3·9 = 27 and 3·8 = 24, all ≥ 20. Count = 10.
solution.misconception: Forgetting that 1 itself is in S (giving 9), or counting 18 twice because it is reachable both as 2·9 and as 3·6. S is a set, so each value counts once.

questions.question: Let S be the smallest set of strings over {0, 1} such that ε ∈ S and, for every w ∈ S, both 0w1 and 1w0 belong to S. Every element of S has equally many 0's and 1's. Which one of the following strings, each with equally many 0's and 1's, does NOT belong to S?
